fullContext:
Dwarkesh Patel: Should we actually begin here? I think this is an interesting discussion.

Ilya Sutskever: Sure.

Dwarkesh Patel: I think your point, about how from the average person's point of view nothing is that different, will continue being true even into the singularity.

Ilya Sutskever: No, I don't think so.
reference: The thing which I was referring to not feeling different is, okay, such and such company announced some difficult-to-comprehend dollar amount of investment. I don't think anyone knows what to do with that. But I think the impact of AI is going to be felt. AI is going to be diffused through the economy. There'll be very strong economic forces for this, and I think the impact is going to be felt very strongly.

astra.text: I think it can feel that way for a while, because a lot of progress can happen somewhere in the background before it affects your life. But at some point, if you really have systems that can do essentially everything people can do, you’re going to feel it. Your work will change. The things that are available to you will change. It’s hard to say exactly how that happens or how quickly. But I don’t think you can have a transformation of that magnitude and have the average person’s life remain basically the same.

r003.rationale: It clearly states that a transformation of this magnitude will be felt by the average person, changing their work and the things available to them.

opus.text:
I think the current period is a strange one, where the thing is very visible intellectually but not yet visible economically. If you look at what's actually happening — the companies are large, the revenue is real, but it's still a small fraction of the economy. So you can live your life, do your job, and the main way AI shows up is that some of your emails are written differently. That's the situation today.

But that's a statement about a particular moment, not about the destination. The destination is: you have computers that can do the work. And when you have computers that can do all the work, you will notice. Everyone will notice. It won't be a subtle thing that you need economists to detect in the statistics five years later. The economy would be growing at a rate that would be unmistakable. Every institution, every job, every question about how society is organized — all of that gets touched.

What I think confuses people is that the lead-up feels gradual, and so they extrapolate the gradualness forever. The models get a bit better, the benchmarks go up, your coding assistant becomes somewhat more useful, and the texture of daily life stays roughly the same. And from that people conclude, well, this is just another technology, it'll diffuse slowly like electricity did. But the reason daily life stays the same right now is that the models are still, in a real sense, not able to learn on the job the way a person does. Once that changes — and I do think it changes — the diffusion is not going to look like electricity. It'll look like something for which we don't have a good analogy.

So no. I think nothing being that different is a true description of 2026, and I would be very surprised if it were a true description of the singularity. Almost by definition.

r001.rationale: The response says computers will do all the work and that every institution and job will be touched, clearly conveying economy-wide diffusion.

r002.rationale: It mentions real revenue and unmistakable economic growth, but does not state that strong economic forces will drive AI's diffusion through the economy.

r003.rationale: The response says everyone will notice, economic growth will be unmistakable, and society's organization will be affected, clearly conveying a very strong impact.

fable.text:
The thing I was referring to is that things aren't that different right now, and I think that's because the AI is still limited. It's impressive, it can do these amazing things, but it isn't really doing economic activity yet. It's not out there in the world doing the work. The diffusion of AI into the economy is slow, slower than people expected, and so you can go about your day and nothing feels different.

But I think that's a temporary situation. Once the AI starts actually doing things—once it's doing the research, once it's running the companies, once there are robots building things, once there's this rapid economic growth that follows from it—I think people will feel it very strongly. It's going to be impossible not to notice. So the current disconnect, where the AI is so much more capable than what the world looks like, I think that disconnect closes. And when it closes, I think it will feel very different. Maybe it will take a while, but it will be felt.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly discusses the diffusion of AI into the economy and describes it spreading through research, companies, and robotic construction.

r002.rationale: It says rapid economic growth will follow AI adoption, but does not state that strong economic forces will drive AI’s diffusion through the economy.

r003.rationale: The response clearly states that AI’s impact will be felt very strongly and will be impossible not to notice.
